whyWrong.B: This is 24x with x taken as −\(\frac{1}{4}\), which comes from subtracting the equations instead of adding them.
whyWrong.C: This is 12x, not 24x — you halved the multiplier, or read the question as asking for 12x.

If line \(k\) is graphed in this xy-plane, resulting in the graph of a system of two linear equations, the system of two linear equations will have infinitely many solutions. What is the value of \(p + w\)?
whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means line \(k\) is line \(g\), so read \(g\) off the graph and force the coefficients to match. From the two marked points, \(g\) has slope \(\frac{1-12}{0-(-9)} = -\frac{11}{9}\) and \(y\)-intercept 1, so \(g\) is \(y = -\frac{11}{9}x + 1\), i.e. 11x + 9y = 9. Line \(k\) is 165x + py = w, and 165 = 15 × 11, so multiply the whole equation of \(g\) by 15: 165x + 135y = 135. That gives p = 135 and w = 135, so p + w = 270.

stem: \[ y = \frac{3}{8}x + 7 \]One of two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has infinitely many solutions. What is the slope of the graph of the second equation?
whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations describe the same line, not two different lines that cross. Same line means same slope, so the second equation's slope is exactly the slope of the given one, \(\frac{3}{8}\).

whyWrong.A: This is the negative reciprocal — the slope of a perpendicular line, which would give exactly one solution.
whyWrong.B: This is the opposite of the slope. Sign-flipping produces a different line, which crosses the given one once.
whyWrong.D: This is the reciprocal. Reciprocals come up when you solve for x in terms of y, not when you match two identical lines.

stem: \[ y = \frac{4}{7}x + 5 \]One of the two equations in a system of linear equations is given. The system has infinitely many solutions. If the second equation in the system is y = mx + b, where m and b are constants, what is the value of b?
whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means the second equation is the same line as the first. Both are written in the form y = mx + b, so the constants must match term for term: m = \(\frac{4}{7}\) and b = 5. The \(\frac{4}{7}\) is not used at all here — b is just the given y-intercept.

whyWrong.A: You negated the intercept. A different intercept gives a parallel line, which has no solutions, not infinitely many.
whyWrong.B: This is the negative reciprocal of 5, an operation nothing in the question calls for.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of 5. Matching identical lines means copying the constant, not inverting it.

whyCorrect: A system with infinitely many solutions is one line written twice, so the second graph has the same slope as the first. The equation is already in y = mx + b form, so the slope is the coefficient of x, \(\frac{5}{7}\).

whyWrong.A: This is the negative reciprocal, the slope of a perpendicular line — that system would have exactly one solution.
whyWrong.B: Flipping the sign gives a different line that crosses the given one once.
whyWrong.D: This is the reciprocal of the slope; you inverted the fraction instead of copying it.

whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means the two equations are the same line. Both are in y = mx + b form, so the constants match directly: b equals the given y-intercept, 3. The \(\frac{2}{7}\) is the value of m and plays no part in finding b.

whyWrong.A: Negating the intercept gives a parallel line, which has no solutions at all.
whyWrong.B: This inverts and negates 3; nothing in the matching of two identical lines does either.
whyWrong.C: This is the reciprocal of 3. You copy the constant, you do not flip it.

stem: The graph of line \(h\) is shown in the xy-plane. Line \(k\) (not shown) is defined by sx + 40y = t, where s and t are constants. If line \(k\) is graphed in this xy-plane, the result is a graph of two linear equations. This system of two linear equations has no solution. Which of the following is NOT a possible value of t?
whyCorrect: No solution means line \(k\) is parallel to \(h\) but is not the same line — that second half is what the question turns on. Line \(h\) runs through (-5, 0) and (0, -8), so its slope is \(-\frac{8}{5}\) and h is 8x + 5y = -40. Matching slopes in sx + 40y = t forces \(-\frac{s}{40} = -\frac{8}{5}\), so s = 64, and multiplying h by 8 gives 64x + 40y = -320. That single value of t makes k identical to h (infinitely many solutions), so t = -320 is the one value ruled out.

whyWrong.A: With s = 64, t = 200 gives a line parallel to h and distinct from it, so the system has no solution — exactly what the question allows.
whyWrong.B: 64 is the value of s, not a forbidden t. As a t value it gives a distinct parallel line, which is fine.
whyWrong.C: t = -8 also gives a distinct parallel line. Any t except -320 works.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: line h passes through (-5, 0) and (0, -8), drawn as a segment across roughly -5 <= x <= 0; grid spans x from -13 to 3 and y from -13 to 7.

whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means one equation is a multiple of the other, so find the multiplier from a coefficient you can see. The y-terms go from 9y to 18y and the constants from 10 to 20, both a factor of 2, so the whole first equation was doubled. Doubling 3x gives r = 6.

whyWrong.A: 2 is the multiplier itself, not the resulting coefficient of x. You still have to apply it to the 3.
whyWrong.B: 3 is the coefficient of x in the first equation, left unmultiplied. That would make the second equation 3x + 18y = 20, which is not proportional to the first.

stem: In the linear function \(g\), \(g(-2) = \frac{3}{4}\) and \(g(3) = \frac{9}{2}\). Which equation defines \(g\)?
whyCorrect: Treat the two function values as two points, \((-2, \frac{3}{4})\) and \((3, \frac{9}{2})\), and find the slope: \(\frac{\frac{9}{2} - \frac{3}{4}}{3 - (-2)} = \frac{\frac{15}{4}}{5} = \frac{3}{4}\). The division by 5 is the step most people drop. Then substitute one point: \(\frac{9}{2} = \frac{3}{4}(3) + b\) gives \(b = \frac{9}{2} - \frac{9}{4} = \frac{9}{4}\).

whyWrong.B: The slope is right but the intercept is the value of \(g(3)\) copied straight in. You still have to subtract \(\frac{3}{4}(3)\) from it.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{15}{4}\) is the rise between the two points, not the slope — you forgot to divide by the run of 5.
whyWrong.D: Same missing division by 5, with the intercept then computed from that wrong slope.

stem: Line \(k\) in the xy-plane has slope \(-\frac{2p}{5}\) and y-intercept \((0, p)\), where \(p\) is a positive constant. What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of line \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Write the line as \(y = -\frac{2p}{5}x + p\) and set \(y = 0\), since that is what an x-intercept means. Then \(\frac{2p}{5}x = p\), and because \(p\) is positive you can divide both sides by it — the \(p\) cancels completely. That leaves \(\frac{2}{5}x = 1\), so \(x = \frac{5}{2}\), a number with no \(p\) in it at all.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = \frac{1}{5}x + \frac{9}{10}. \]For what value of x does \(f(x) = 1\)?
whyCorrect: Set the expression equal to 1 and solve: \(\frac{1}{5}x + \frac{9}{10} = 1\), so \(\frac{1}{5}x = \frac{1}{10}\). Multiplying both sides by 5 gives \(x = \frac{1}{2}\). If fractions slow you down, multiply the whole equation by 10 first: 2x + 9 = 10.

Her rate is therefore 60 ÷ 12 = 5 flowers per hour. The slope of the line is not the answer — it compares the two people's times, not flowers per hour.

whyWrong.C: 12 is the number of hours Lucia needs, not the number of flowers she makes in one hour. You still have to divide 60 by it.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x) = \frac{x + 11}{3}\), and \(f(a) = 16\), where a is a constant. What is the value of a?
whyCorrect: \(f(a) = 16\) just means you put a into the rule and the output is 16: \(\frac{a + 11}{3} = 16\). Undo the division first, not the addition — multiply both sides by 3 to get a + 11 = 48, then subtract 11 for a = 37.

whyWrong.A: This undoes the operations in the wrong order: subtracting 11 from 16 and then multiplying by 3 would be the route to 15, and 9 comes from dividing 27 by 3. Either way the multiplication by 3 has to come first.
whyWrong.B: 16 is the output f(a), not the input a. The two are only equal if the function does nothing.
whyWrong.C: This adds 11 to 48 instead of subtracting it. Since the rule adds 11 before dividing, you subtract to undo it.

Perpendicular lines have slopes whose product is -1, so line \(k\) has slope \(-\frac{1}{5}\) — flip the fraction and change the sign, not one or the other.

whyWrong.B: You flipped and negated a slope of 6, which comes from misreading the y-intercept as 6 instead of 5.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the slope of line n itself. A perpendicular line cannot have the same slope.
whyWrong.D: This is a misread slope for n, and it is not perpendicular either.

stem: A publishing company is preparing boxes of workbooks and textbooks for shipping. Each box of workbooks and textbooks will weigh a total of 40 pounds. The graph shown models the relationship between the number of textbooks x and the number of workbooks y that can be shipped in 1 box. Based on the graph, what is the weight, in pounds, of 1 textbook?
whyCorrect: Use the intercept that removes the workbooks. The line meets the x-axis at (10, 0): 10 textbooks and no workbooks fill a 40-pound box, so one textbook weighs 40 ÷ 10 = 4 pounds. Reading the y-intercept instead gives the workbook weight, which is not what is asked.

whyWrong.A: Negative weight is impossible; this comes from treating a slope or a difference of intercepts as a weight.
whyWrong.B: 10 is the number of textbooks that fill a box, not the weight of one. You still have to divide 40 by it.
whyWrong.D: 2 pounds is the weight of one workbook, from the y-intercept of 20: 40 ÷ 20 = 2. You read the wrong axis.

stem: How many solutions \((x, y)\) does the system of three linear equations represented in the graph have?
whyCorrect: A solution to the system has to satisfy all three equations at once, so it must be a point every line passes through. The two steep lines have the same slope and different intercepts, so they are parallel and share no point at all. It does not matter that the horizontal line crosses each of them — there is no point common to all three, so the system has 0 solutions.

whyWrong.B: There is no single point on all three lines; the two parallel lines never meet each other.
whyWrong.C: 2 counts the crossings visible on the graph (the horizontal line meets each steep line once). Those are intersections of pairs, not solutions of the three-equation system.
whyWrong.D: 3 assumes each pair of lines contributes a crossing, but the two parallel lines contribute none, and pairwise crossings are not solutions of the system anyway.

stem: The total amount of food y in pounds that a zookeeper feeds a giraffe over x days is represented by the equation y = 30x. What is the total amount of food, in pounds, that the zookeeper feeds the giraffe over 3 days?
whyCorrect: x counts days, so substitute x = 3 into the equation you were given: y = 30(3) = 90 pounds. Nothing else in the equation changes — there is no fixed starting amount to add.

whyWrong.A: 30 is the amount for a single day, x = 1. You have to multiply by the 3 days.
whyWrong.B: This adds 3 to 30. The 30 multiplies the number of days, it is not a starting total that days get added to.
whyWrong.D: This multiplies correctly and then adds an extra 3 that the equation does not contain.

stem: The graph of the linear equation \[ 15x + By = 60 \]is shown, where B is a constant. What is the value of B?
whyCorrect: Read the y-intercept off the graph — the line meets the y-axis at (0, 3) — and substitute that point into the equation: 15(0) + B(3) = 60, so 3B = 60 and B = 20. (The x-intercept is no help here: setting y = 0 gives 15x = 60, or x = 4, with B cancelling out entirely.)

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{3}{4}\) is the size of the line's slope, read off the graph rather than substituted into the equation.
whyWrong.B: 3 is the y-intercept itself. It is the value of y at that point, not the coefficient multiplying y.
whyWrong.C: 4 is the x-intercept, which is 60 ÷ 15 and tells you nothing about B.

stem: The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x) = \frac{4}{5}x - 32\). What is the x-coordinate of the x-intercept of the graph of \(y = g(x)\) in the xy-plane?
whyCorrect: An x-intercept is where y = 0, so set the whole expression equal to 0: \(\frac{4}{5}x - 32 = 0\). That gives \(\frac{4}{5}x = 32\), and multiplying by the reciprocal \(\frac{5}{4}\) gives x = 40. Dividing by \(\frac{4}{5}\) is the same as multiplying by \(\frac{5}{4}\) — that is where a wrong answer of 25.6 comes from.

stem: Line \(k\) is shown in the xy-plane. Line \(n\) (not shown) is perpendicular to line \(k\) and passes through the point (2, 9). Which equation defines line \(n\)?
whyCorrect: Line \(k\) rises 2 for every 3 across — it passes through (-8, -8) and (4, 0) — so its slope is \(\frac{2}{3}\) and the perpendicular slope is \(-\frac{3}{2}\). That rules out C and D immediately. Then force the line through (2, 9): \(9 = -\frac{3}{2}(2) + b\) gives \(9 = -3 + b\), so b = 12.

whyWrong.A: The slope is right, but the intercept was found with the wrong sign: \(9 = \frac{3}{2}(2) + b\) gives 6. Substituting x = 2 into \(-\frac{3}{2}x\) gives -3, so b = 12.
whyWrong.C: This is the negative reciprocal with the sign left unchanged, so it is not perpendicular to k.
whyWrong.D: Same sign error on the slope, and (2, 9) does not satisfy it: \(\frac{3}{2}(2) - 3 = 0\), not 9.

stem: What is the slope of the graph of \[ 8x - 4y = -12 \]in the xy-plane?
whyCorrect: Solve for y so the slope is the coefficient of x: \(-4y = -8x - 12\), then divide every term by -4 to get y = 2x + 3. Both signs flip when you divide by a negative, which is exactly the step that produces the wrong sign if you rush it.

whyWrong.A: You divided by -4 on the left but not the right, or dropped one of the two sign changes. The negatives cancel here.
whyWrong.B: This mixes up the coefficients, dividing 8 by -12 rather than solving for y.
whyWrong.C: Same coefficient mix-up, with the sign corrected. The slope comes from y = mx + b, not from a ratio of the two constants.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x) = \frac{x}{10} + 74\). What is the value of \(f(20)\)?
whyCorrect: Substitute 20 wherever x appears: \(\frac{20}{10} + 74 = 2 + 74 = 76\). Divide before you add — the 74 is not part of the fraction.

stem: \[ g(m) = -0.05m + 14.1 \]The given function \(g\) models the number of gallons of gasoline that remains from a full gas tank in a car after driving m miles. According to the model, about how many gallons of gasoline are used to drive each mile?

stem: The graph of \(y = f(x)\) is shown. What is the y-intercept of the graph of \(y = f(x) + 13\)?
whyCorrect: Adding 13 to a function shifts every point up by 13, so the y-intercept moves up by 13 and stays on the y-axis. The graph shows f(0) = 1, so the new intercept is at (0, 1 + 13) = (0, 14). Only the y-value changes; x stays 0.

whyWrong.A: This subtracts 13 from 1 instead of adding. Adding a positive constant raises the graph.
whyWrong.C: This puts the 1 in the x-slot. An intercept on the y-axis always has x = 0; the 1 was the height, not a horizontal position.
whyWrong.D: This assumes f(0) = 0, reading the intercept at the origin. The line crosses the y-axis one unit above it.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x + 8). \]What is the value of \(f(10)\)?
whyCorrect: Work inside the parentheses first: 10 + 8 = 18, then halve it to get 9. The \(\frac{1}{2}\) multiplies the whole sum, not just the x.

whyWrong.A: This doubles 18 instead of halving it — multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2}\) is division by 2, not by \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.B: 18 is the value inside the parentheses. You still have to multiply by \(\frac{1}{2}\).

The function f(m) = 30 − 6m gives the amount of money, in dollars, in the account after the family has rented m movies. Which of the following represents the amount of money, in dollars, withdrawn from the account each time the family rents a movie?
whyCorrect: Each extra rental increases m by 1 and drops the balance by 6, so the cost of one rental is the coefficient of m: 6 dollars. The question asks for the amount per rental, which is a fixed number, not something that depends on m.

whyWrong.A: 6m is the total withdrawn after m rentals, not the cost of a single one.
whyWrong.C: 30 is the starting balance, the value when m = 0, before any movie is rented.
whyWrong.D: This is the whole function — the money left in the account, not the money taken out.

stem: For the linear function \(f\), the graph of \(y = f(x)\) in the xy-plane has a slope of \(\frac{4}{5}\) and passes through the point (20, 19). Which equation defines \(f\)?
whyCorrect: Every choice already has the right slope, so all you need is b. Substitute the point into \(y = \frac{4}{5}x + b\): \(19 = \frac{4}{5}(20) + b = 16 + b\), so b = 3.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{19}{20}\) is the two coordinates divided. A point is substituted into the equation, not turned into a fraction.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{24}{5}\) is what you get with the coordinates swapped: \(20 - \frac{4}{5}(19) = \frac{24}{5}\). The point is (20, 19), so x = 20.
whyWrong.C: This uses the y-coordinate 19 as the intercept, which is only valid if the point sits on the y-axis. Here x = 20, so you must subtract the 16 that the slope contributes.

stem: \[ F(x) = \frac{9}{5}(x - 273.15) + 32 \]The function \(F\) gives the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, that corresponds to x kelvins. If a temperature is increased by 11.70 kelvins, by how much did the temperature increase in degrees Fahrenheit?
whyCorrect: You are asked for a change, not a temperature, so only the rate matters: every 1 kelvin of increase adds \(\frac{9}{5}\) degrees Fahrenheit. The -273.15 and the +32 shift where the scale starts and cancel out of any difference. So the increase is \(\frac{9}{5}(11.70) = 21.06\) degrees Fahrenheit.

stem: For the linear function \(f\), the graph \(y = f(x)\) in the xy-plane has a slope of \(\frac{2}{3}\) and passes through the point (6, 5). Which equation defines \(f\)?
whyCorrect: All four choices share the slope, so only the constant is in question. Substitute the point into \(y = \frac{2}{3}x + b\): \(5 = \frac{2}{3}(6) + b = 4 + b\), so b = 1.

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{5}{6}\) is the coordinates divided into a fraction, which is not what substitution does.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{8}{3}\) comes from swapping the coordinates: \(6 - \frac{2}{3}(5) = \frac{8}{3}\). In (6, 5) the 6 is x.
whyWrong.C: This treats the y-coordinate 5 as the intercept. That only works for a point already on the y-axis; here you must subtract the 4 the slope contributes.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by f(x) = 10x + 8. What is the value of \(f(x)\) when x = 7?
whyCorrect: Substitute 7 for x: 10(7) + 8 = 70 + 8 = 78. Multiply before you add.

whyWrong.A: This adds 10 + 8 + 7. The 10 multiplies x, it does not get added to it.
whyWrong.B: An arithmetic slip: 10(7) is 70, and 70 + 8 is 78, not 66.
whyWrong.D: This swaps the 8 and the 7, computing 10(8) + 7. The value substituted for x is 7.

stem: Scientists collected fallen acorns that each housed a colony of the ant species P. ohioensis and analyzed each colony's structure. For any of these colonies, if the colony has x worker ants, the equation y = 0.67x + 2.6, where 20 ≤ x ≤ 110, gives the predicted number of larvae y in the colony. If one of these colonies has 46 worker ants, which of the following is closest to the predicted number of larvae in the colony?
whyCorrect: x is the number of worker ants, so substitute 46: y = 0.67(46) + 2.6 = 30.82 + 2.6 = 33.42. The closest choice is 33.

whyWrong.B: 49 is roughly 46 + 2.6 with the 0.67 ignored, treating the ant count as if it carried straight over.
whyWrong.C: 65 is about 46 ÷ 0.67 — dividing by the rate instead of multiplying by it. That would answer the reverse question, how many workers go with 46 larvae.
whyWrong.D: 150 is far outside the model's range for x = 46; no combination of the given numbers produces it.

note: The book misprints the fourth choice's letter as C, so two choices are labelled C; the value 150 is transcribed here as D.

stem: \[ f(x) = 5x + b \]For the linear function \(f\), b is a constant and \(f(7) = 35\). What is the value of b?
whyCorrect: Substitute x = 7 and set the result equal to 35: 5(7) + b = 35, so 35 + b = 35 and b = 0. A constant of 0 is a legitimate answer — it just means the line passes through the origin.

whyWrong.B: 1 would make f(7) = 36. Check by substituting back.
whyWrong.C: 5 is the slope, already accounted for by the 5x term.
whyWrong.D: 7 is the input value, not the constant; it is what you substitute for x.

stem: At a depth of h meters below the surface, the estimated total pressure \(P_1\), in kilopascals (kPa), a diver experienced is given by \(P_1 = 10h + 101\), which is a combination of estimated water pressure and estimated atmospheric pressure. After maintaining a certain depth, the diver descended d additional meters. The estimated total pressure \(P_2\), in kPa, that the diver experienced after descending these d additional meters is given by \(P_2 = 10d + 311\). Which of the following is the best interpretation of 311 in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The estimated total pressure, in kPa, the diver experienced at a depth of d meters.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The estimated increase in the total pressure, in kPa, the diver experienced for each increase in the depth by 1 meter.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The estimated increase in the total pressure, in kPa, the diver experienced for each increase in the depth by d meters.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The estimated total pressure, in kPa, the diver experienced when the diver began to descend d additional meters.

whyCorrect: A constant term is the value of the expression when the variable is 0, so ask what d = 0 means here: the diver has not yet descended any of the additional meters. So 311 kPa is the pressure at the depth the diver was already holding, right before the extra descent began.

whyWrong.A: d measures the additional descent, not depth below the surface, and the pressure at d additional meters is the whole expression 10d + 311, not the constant alone.
whyWrong.B: That is the 10, the rate of change per metre. 311 does not change with d.
whyWrong.C: Also a description of the rate, and applied over d metres it would be 10d — still not the constant.

stem: Line \(k\) is defined by \(y = 6x + \frac{1}{9}\). Line \(j\) is perpendicular to line \(k\) in the xy-plane. What is the slope of line \(j\)?
whyCorrect: The slope of k is the coefficient of x, which is 6 — the \(\frac{1}{9}\) is the intercept and is irrelevant here. A perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal, so flip 6 to \(\frac{1}{6}\) and change the sign: \(-\frac{1}{6}\).

whyWrong.A: This takes the negative reciprocal of the intercept \(\frac{1}{9}\) instead of the slope.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{1}{9}\) is k's y-intercept copied over, and it is not perpendicular to anything.
whyWrong.D: 6 is k's own slope; a line with the same slope is parallel to k, not perpendicular.

stem: What is an equation of the graph shown?
whyCorrect: All four choices have the same intercept, 12, so the graph settles it on slope alone. The line falls as you move right, so the slope is negative, and it drops from 12 at x = 0 to 2 at x = 10 — 10 down over 10 across, a slope of -1.

whyWrong.A: Slope +1 rises to the right; the graphed line falls.
whyWrong.C: Slope 2 rises, and twice as steeply as the graph.
whyWrong.D: The sign is right but the line is twice too steep: a slope of -2 would reach y = -8 at x = 10, not y = 2.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: the line y = -x + 12 drawn over roughly -4 <= x <= 10; grid spans x from -11 to 11 and y from -16 to 16.

stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = \frac{7}{10}x + 61. \]What is the value of \(f(20)\)?
whyCorrect: Substitute 20 for x: \(\frac{7}{10}(20) = 14\), then add 61 to get 75. Multiply the fraction by 20 first — the 61 is outside it.

stem: A certain open star cluster contains M-type stars and K-type stars. The estimated total mass of all M-type and K-type stars in this open star cluster is 132,778 quettagrams. The graph shown models the possible combinations of the number of M-type stars, x, and K-type stars, y, that could be in this open star cluster if all the M-type stars have the same estimated mass and all the K-type stars have the same estimated mass. Based on the graph, which of the following is closest to the estimated mass, in quettagrams, of each M-type star in this cluster?
whyCorrect: Use the intercept that removes the other kind of star. Where the line meets the x-axis there are no K-type stars, so about 160 M-type stars account for the entire 132,778 quettagrams: 132,778 ÷ 160 ≈ 830, closest to 828. The y-intercept would give the K-type mass instead.

whyWrong.B: 973 comes from the y-intercept of about 137: 132,778 ÷ 137 is the mass of one K-type star, not an M-type.
whyWrong.C: This is the total mass divided by about 2.5, or a slope misread; it is far too large for one star when 160 of them share the total.
whyWrong.D: This is roughly half the total mass, which would only be one star's mass if the cluster held two stars.

note: Depends on a graph. Verified data for rebuilding it: a segment from about (0, 137) to about (160, 0); x-axis 'Number of M-type stars' 0 to about 170, y-axis 'Number of K-type stars' 0 to about 165. The book's y-axis label misprints K-type as N-type.

stem: Lines \(h\) and \(k\) are graphed in the xy-plane. The graph of line \(h\) has a slope of \(\frac{5}{3}\) and an x-intercept at (17, 0). Line \(k\) is the result of translating the graph of line \(h\) down 4 units. What is the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the graph of line \(k\)?
whyCorrect: Build h from the point and slope: \(y = \frac{5}{3}(x - 17)\), so at x = 0 its y-intercept is \(-\frac{85}{3}\). Translating down 4 units subtracts 4 from every y-value and leaves the slope alone, so k's intercept is \(-\frac{85}{3} - 4 = -\frac{85}{3} - \frac{12}{3} = -\frac{97}{3}\), about -32.33. A common slip is shifting the x-intercept by 4 instead of the y-values.

stem: \[ g(m) = -0.04m + 16.6 \]The given function \(g\) models the number of gallons of gasoline that remains from a full gas tank in a car after driving m miles. According to the model, about how many gallons of gasoline are used to drive each mile?
whyCorrect: The coefficient of m tells you how the amount remaining changes per extra mile: -0.04 gallons. Fuel used per mile is the size of that drop, 0.04 gallons; the minus sign only says the tank is emptying.

whyWrong.B: 16.6 is the value at m = 0 — the size of a full tank, not a rate.
whyWrong.C: 25 is \(\frac{1}{0.04}\), the miles the car travels per gallon. That is the reciprocal of what was asked.
whyWrong.D: 415.0 is 16.6 × 25, the total distance a full tank covers, not a per-mile amount.

stem: \[ w(t) = 600 - 8t \]The function \(w\) models the volume of water, in milliliters, in a container t seconds after it begins draining from a hole at the bottom. According to the model, what is the predicted volume, in milliliters, draining from the container each second?
whyCorrect: Each extra second subtracts 8 from the volume left, so 8 millilitres drain per second. The rate is the coefficient of t, not a volume read off the function.

whyWrong.B: 75 is 600 ÷ 8, the number of seconds the container takes to empty — a time, not a volume per second.
whyWrong.C: 592 is w(1), the volume still in the container after one second. The amount that drained is 600 - 592 = 8.
whyWrong.D: 600 is the starting volume, the value at t = 0.

stem: A hemisphere and a cone have circular bases of equal circumference and have been connected at their bases, as shown in the figure. The diameter of the base of the hemisphere is 6 centimeters (cm) and the total height of the figure is 9 cm. What is the total volume, in \(\text{cm}^3\), of the cone and hemisphere?
whyCorrect: Split the 9 cm of total height between the two solids. The radius is half of 6, so r = 3, and a hemisphere of radius 3 is 3 cm tall — that leaves 9 - 3 = 6 cm for the cone's height. Then the hemisphere is \(\frac{2}{3}\pi(3)^3 = 18\pi\) and the cone is \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(3)^2(6) = 18\pi\), for a total of \(36\pi\).

whyWrong.A: \(18\pi\) is just one of the two pieces; both happen to equal \(18\pi\), so stopping after one halves the answer.
whyWrong.C: \(45\pi\) comes from giving the cone the full 9 cm of height: \(\frac{1}{3}\pi(9)(9) = 27\pi\) plus \(18\pi\). The hemisphere occupies the top 3 cm.
whyWrong.D: \(162\pi\) treats the whole shape as a cylinder of radius 3 and height 9 × 2, or drops the \(\frac{1}{3}\) and \(\frac{2}{3}\) factors entirely.

note: Stem refers to a figure. Verified data for rebuilding it: a hemisphere (flat face down, radius 3 cm) sitting on top of a cone that points downward, sharing the circular base; a vertical dimension arrow at the right labelled 9 cm spanning the whole shape.

stem: The area of a triangle is equal to \(x^2\) square centimeters. The length of the base of the triangle is 2x + 6 centimeters, and the height of the triangle is x − 2 centimeters. What is the value of x?
whyCorrect: Write the area two ways and set them equal: \(x^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 6)(x - 2)\). Halving the base first makes the algebra easy: \(\frac{1}{2}(2x+6) = x + 3\), so the right side is \((x + 3)(x - 2) = x^2 + x - 6\). The \(x^2\) terms cancel, leaving x - 6 = 0, so x = 6 (base 18, height 4, area 36).

stem: A right circular cylinder has a height of 4 meters (m) and a base with a radius of 18 m. What is the volume, in \(\text{m}^3\), of the cylinder?
whyCorrect: Volume of a cylinder is \(\pi r^2 h\). Square the radius before multiplying by the height: \(\pi(18)^2(4) = \pi(324)(4) = 1296\pi\).

whyWrong.A: This is the height alone; the base area is missing.
whyWrong.B: This adds 18 and 4 instead of using \(\pi r^2 h\).
whyWrong.C: This swaps the radius and the height: \(\pi(4)^2(18) = 288\pi\). The radius is the number that gets squared.

stem: The volume of a right rectangular prism with a square base is 2,448 cubic centimeters. If the area of the square base is 144 square centimeters, what is the area, in square centimeters, of one of the four lateral faces of the prism?
whyCorrect: A lateral face is a rectangle whose sides are the base edge and the height, so you need both. The base edge is \(\sqrt{144} = 12\), and since volume = base area × height, the height is 2,448 ÷ 144 = 17. One lateral face is therefore 12 × 17 = 204.

whyWrong.A: 17 is the height of the prism, only one dimension of the face. Multiply it by the 12 cm edge.
whyWrong.C: 540 does not come out of any of these numbers; check that you found the edge as \(\sqrt{144}\) and the height as 2,448 ÷ 144.
whyWrong.D: 816 is all four lateral faces together, 4 × 204. The question asks for one of them.

stem: The volume of a right rectangular prism with a square base is 1,792 cubic centimeters. If the area of the square base is 64 square centimeters, what is the area, in square centimeters, of one of the four lateral faces of the prism?
whyCorrect: The base edge is \(\sqrt{64} = 8\), and the height is volume ÷ base area = 1,792 ÷ 64 = 28. A lateral face is a rectangle 8 by 28, so its area is 224.

whyWrong.A: 28 is the height alone, not an area. It still has to be multiplied by the 8 cm base edge.
whyWrong.C: 416 is not produced by any correct combination here; the two numbers you need are 8 and 28.
whyWrong.D: 896 is the four lateral faces added together, 4 × 224. Only one face was asked for.

stem: The area of a rectangle is 630 square inches. The length of the rectangle is 90 inches. What is the width, in inches, of this rectangle?
whyCorrect: Area = length × width, so width = 630 ÷ 90 = 7.

whyWrong.B: 90 is the length you were given, not the width.
whyWrong.C: 315 is half the area, which would be the width only if the length were 2.
whyWrong.D: 540 is 630 - 90. Area is a product of the sides, so you divide to undo it, not subtract.

stem: The length of the diagonal of a square is \(\frac{148\sqrt{2}}{2}\) units. What is the area, in square units, of the square?
whyCorrect: Simplify first: \(\frac{148\sqrt{2}}{2} = 74\sqrt{2}\). A square's diagonal is \(s\sqrt{2}\), so \(s\sqrt{2} = 74\sqrt{2}\) gives a side of 74, and the area is \(74^2 = 5{,}476\).

whyWrong.A: 74 is the side length, not the area. Square it.
whyWrong.B: 296 is 4 × 74, the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: 10,952 is the diagonal squared, \((74\sqrt{2})^2\). For a square that is twice the area — the area is \(\frac{d^2}{2}\).

stem: The floor of a school has an area of 2,025 square meters. An architect creates a scale model of the floor of the school, where the length of each side of the model is \(\frac{1}{15}\) times the length of the corresponding side of the actual floor of the school. What is the area, in square meters, of the scale model?
whyCorrect: Areas scale by the square of the length factor, because both dimensions shrink. Each side is \(\frac{1}{15}\) as long, so the area is \(\left(\frac{1}{15}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{225}\) as large: 2,025 ÷ 225 = 9.

whyWrong.B: 15 is the scale factor itself, not an area.
whyWrong.C: 135 is 2,025 ÷ 15, dividing by the length factor once. Both length and width shrink, so you divide twice.
whyWrong.D: 225 is \(15^2\), the factor you divide by, not the resulting area.

The table shows the volume of two similar solids, right circular cylinder \(A\) and right circular cylinder \(B\). The radius of right circular cylinder \(A\) is 4 units. The surface area of right circular cylinder \(A\) is \(k\pi\) square units, and the surface area of right circular cylinder \(B\) is \(n\pi\) square units, where k and n are constants. What is the value of \(n - k\)? (The surface area of a right circular cylinder with radius r and height h is \(2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh\).)
whyCorrect: Get cylinder A completely, then scale. From \(\pi(4)^2h = 112\pi\) the height is 7, so A's surface area is \(2\pi(16) + 2\pi(4)(7) = 88\pi\), giving k = 88. For similar solids the volume ratio is the cube of the length ratio: \(\frac{3024}{112} = 27\), so lengths scale by 3 and areas scale by \(3^2 = 9\). Then n = 9(88) = 792, and n - k = 792 - 88 = 704.

stem: Each side of square \(A\) has a length of 11 inches. Each side of square \(A\) is multiplied by a scale factor of 3 to create square \(B\). What is the length, in inches, of each side of square \(B\)?
whyCorrect: A scale factor multiplies each length: 11 × 3 = 33 inches.

whyWrong.A: This subtracts 3 from 11. A scale factor multiplies.
whyWrong.B: 11 is square A's side, unchanged.
whyWrong.C: This adds 3 to 11 instead of multiplying.

stem: The width of a rectangle is 7 centimeters. The length of the rectangle is 40 centimeters longer than the width. What is the area, in square centimeters, of this rectangle?
whyCorrect: "40 longer than the width" means length = 7 + 40 = 47, not 40. Then the area is 47 × 7 = 329 square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 7 is the width by itself.
whyWrong.B: 14 is twice the width; no multiplication by the length has happened.
whyWrong.C: 54 is 7 + 47, the length plus the width (half the perimeter), not their product.

stem: The length of the diagonal of a square is \(\frac{158\sqrt{2}}{2}\) units. What is the area, in square units, of the square?
whyCorrect: Simplify the diagonal first: \(\frac{158\sqrt{2}}{2} = 79\sqrt{2}\). A square with side s has diagonal \(s\sqrt{2}\), so s = 79 and the area is \(79^2 = 6241\).

whyWrong.A: 79 is the side length; the question asks for the area.
whyWrong.B: 316 is 4 × 79, the perimeter.
whyWrong.D: 12,482 is the diagonal squared. For a square the area is \(\frac{d^2}{2}\), so this is double the area.

stem: The floor of a school has an area of 4400 square meters. An architect creates a scale model of the floor of the school, where the length of each side of the model is \(\frac{1}{20}\) times the length of the corresponding sides of the actual floor of the school. What is the area, in square meters, of the scale model?
whyCorrect: Both dimensions shrink by \(\frac{1}{20}\), so the area shrinks by \(\left(\frac{1}{20}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{400}\). That gives 4,400 ÷ 400 = 11 square meters.

whyWrong.B: 20 is the scale factor, not an area.
whyWrong.C: 220 is 4,400 ÷ 20, applying the length factor only once instead of to both dimensions.
whyWrong.D: 275 is 4,400 ÷ 16, which uses a factor of 4 rather than 20.

stem: A sphere has a radius of \(\frac{13}{5}\) feet. What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the sphere?
whyCorrect: Use \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\) and cube the whole fraction, top and bottom: \(\left(\frac{13}{5}\right)^3 = \frac{2197}{125}\). Then \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot \frac{2197}{125} = \frac{8788\pi}{375}\).

whyWrong.B: This does not come from the volume formula; nothing here produces a denominator of 5 once the radius is cubed.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{52\pi}{15}\) is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r\) — the radius was never cubed.
whyWrong.D: This is the reciprocal of the radius times \(\pi\), with the formula ignored.

stem: Rectangles \(ABCD\) and \(EFGH\) are similar. The length of each side of \(EFGH\) is 6 times the length of the corresponding side of \(ABCD\). The area of \(ABCD\) is 96 square units. What is the area, in square units, of \(EFGH\)?
whyCorrect: Both dimensions are 6 times longer, so the area grows by \(6^2 = 36\), not by 6. That gives 96 × 36 = 3,456 square units.

whyWrong.A: 16 is 96 ÷ 6 — shrinking instead of enlarging, and by the length factor rather than its square.
whyWrong.B: 36 is the area factor itself, not the new area. It still has to multiply 96.
whyWrong.C: 576 is 96 × 6, scaling by the length factor once. A second dimension also grew by 6.

stem: Rectangle \(ABCD\) is similar to rectangle \(EFGH\). The area of rectangle \(ABCD\) is 648 square inches, and the area of rectangle \(EFGH\) is 72 square inches. The length of the longest side of rectangle \(ABCD\) is 36 inches. What is the length, in inches, of the longest side of rectangle \(EFGH\)?
whyCorrect: The areas are in the ratio \(\frac{648}{72} = 9\), and for similar figures the area ratio is the square of the length ratio. So lengths are in the ratio \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), and the longest side of EFGH is 36 ÷ 3 = 12 inches.

whyWrong.A: 4 is 36 ÷ 9, dividing by the area ratio instead of its square root.
whyWrong.B: 9 is the ratio of the areas, not a length.
whyWrong.D: 36 is ABCD's side. EFGH is the smaller rectangle, so its longest side must be shorter.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a length of 26 centimeters (cm), a width of 16 cm, and a height of 14 cm. What is the surface area, in \(\text{cm}^2\), of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: A box has three distinct face shapes, each appearing twice, so the surface area is 2(lw + lh + wh). Here that is 2(26·16 + 26·14 + 16·14) = 2(416 + 364 + 224) = 2(1,004) = 2,008 square centimeters. Forgetting the factor of 2 gives 1,004; multiplying all three dimensions gives the volume instead.

stem: Rectangle \(ABCD\) and \(EFGH\) are similar. The length of each side of \(EFGH\) is 10 times the length of the corresponding side of \(ABCD\). The area of \(ABCD\) is 100 square units. What is the area, in square units, of \(EFGH\)?
whyCorrect: Length scales by 10 and width scales by 10, so the area scales by \(10^2 = 100\). That gives 100 × 100 = 10,000 square units.

whyWrong.A: 10 is the length factor, not an area.
whyWrong.B: 100 is the original area, unchanged.
whyWrong.C: 1,000 is 100 × 10, applying the factor to only one dimension.

stem: The floor of a library has an area of 9375 square feet. An architect creates a scale model of the floor of the library, where the length of each side of the model is \(\frac{1}{25}\) times the length of the corresponding side of the floor of the actual library. What is the area, in square feet, of the scale model?
whyCorrect: Area scales by the square of the length factor, since both dimensions shrink: \(\left(\frac{1}{25}\right)^2 = \frac{1}{625}\). So the model's area is 9,375 ÷ 625 = 15 square feet. Dividing by 25 only once gives 375, which is the common wrong answer.

stem: A right square pyramid has a total surface area of 36,864 square inches, and the combined surface area of the four lateral faces of this pyramid is 20,480 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
whyCorrect: Work back through three steps. The base is what is left of the total: 36,864 - 20,480 = 16,384 square inches, so the base edge is \(\sqrt{16384} = 128\). The four lateral faces are triangles of base 128 and slant height \(\ell\), so \(4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(128)\ell = 256\ell = 20{,}480\), giving \(\ell = 80\). Finally the slant height, the height, and half the base edge form a right triangle: \(h = \sqrt{80^2 - 64^2} = \sqrt{2304} = 48\).

whyWrong.B: 64 is half the base edge, the horizontal leg of that right triangle, not the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: 80 is the slant height — the height of a triangular face, measured along the slanted surface, not straight up from the centre of the base.
whyWrong.D: 128 is the base edge itself.

stem: The figure shown is a right circular cylinder with a radius r and a height of h. A second right circular cylinder (not shown) has a volume that is 576 times as large as the volume of the cylinder shown. Which of the following could represent the radius R, in terms of r, and the height H, in terms of h, of the second cylinder?
whyCorrect: In \(V = \pi r^2 h\) the radius is squared but the height is not, so scaling the radius by a and the height by b multiplies the volume by \(a^2 b\). Test the choices: \(8^2 \times 9 = 64 \times 9 = 576\), which is the required factor.

whyWrong.A: \(9^2 \times 8 = 648\), not 576. Here the larger factor was put on the radius, where squaring makes it too big.
whyWrong.B: \(9^2 \times 64 = 5{,}184\), nine times too large.
whyWrong.D: \(64^2 \times 9 = 36{,}864\). The 64 belongs to the squared effect of scaling the radius by 8, not to the radius itself.

note: Stem refers to a figure. It is only a generic labelled diagram: a right circular cylinder with a horizontal radius segment marked r on the top face and a vertical arrow at the right marked h. No measurements appear in it.

stem: A right circular cone has a volume of \(2{,}700\pi\) cubic centimeters and the area of its base is \(225\pi\) square centimeters. What is the slant height, in centimeters, of this cone?
whyCorrect: Get the radius from the base area: \(\pi r^2 = 225\pi\) gives r = 15. Then from \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h\): \(\frac{1}{3}(225\pi)h = 2700\pi\), so 75h = 2,700 and h = 36. The slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by r and h: \(\sqrt{15^2 + 36^2} = \sqrt{1521} = 39\).

whyWrong.A: 12 is smaller than both legs, so it cannot be the hypotenuse of that triangle.
whyWrong.B: 15 is the radius, one leg of the triangle.
whyWrong.C: 36 is the vertical height, the other leg. The slant height runs up the surface and is longer than either.

stem: The volume of a right rectangular prism with a square base is 539 cubic centimeters. If the area of each of the four lateral faces is 77 square centimeters, what is the height, in centimeters, of the prism?
whyCorrect: Call the base edge s and the height h. Then \(s^2h = 539\) and \(sh = 77\). Dividing the first by the second cancels h and gives s = 539 ÷ 77 = 7. Substituting back, 7h = 77, so h = 11.

whyWrong.A: 77 is the area of one lateral face, not a length.
whyWrong.B: 49 is \(s^2\), the area of the square base.
whyWrong.D: 7 is the base edge s. The question asks for the height, which is the other factor in the 77.

stem: A right triangular pyramid has exactly six edges. Each of these edges is 96 centimeters long. If the surface area of the pyramid is \(k\sqrt{3}\) square centimeters, what is the value of k?
whyCorrect: Six equal edges means all four faces are equilateral triangles of side 96. One such triangle has area \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^2 = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}(9216) = 2304\sqrt{3}\), and there are four faces — the base counts too. So the surface area is \(4(2304\sqrt{3}) = 9216\sqrt{3}\), and k = 9,216. Note the 4 in the formula cancels the four faces, so k is simply \(96^2\).

stem: The height of a right circular cylinder is 6 inches longer than its radius, and the surface area of the cylinder is \(1080\pi\) square inches. What is the cylinder's radius, in inches?
whyCorrect: Write the height as r + 6 and substitute into \(2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh\): \(2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r(r+6) = 1080\pi\). Divide out \(\pi\) and collect: \(4r^2 + 12r - 1080 = 0\), or \(r^2 + 3r - 270 = 0\), which factors as (r + 18)(r - 15) = 0. A radius cannot be negative, so r = 15 (and the height is 21). Checking with the choices is faster than factoring if you spot it.

whyWrong.B: 18 comes from the discarded root -18 with its sign flipped; substituting 18 gives a surface area of \(1512\pi\).
whyWrong.C: 21 is the height, r + 6, not the radius.
whyWrong.D: 24 makes the surface area \(2\pi(576) + 2\pi(24)(30) = 2592\pi\), far too large.

note: The book writes "right-angular cylinder" and "surface are"; transcribed as right circular cylinder and surface area.

stem: A right rectangular prism has a base of 28p square centimeters (\(\text{cm}^2\)). The length of the rectangular prism is 12 cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 4 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in \(\text{cm}^2\), of the right rectangular prism?
whyCorrect: Find the missing width first. The base is a rectangle of area 28p with length 12, so the width is \(\frac{28p}{12} = \frac{7p}{3}\). Surface area is 2(base) + perimeter of base × height: \(2(28p) + 2\left(12 + \frac{7p}{3}\right)(4) = 56p + 96 + \frac{56p}{3} = \frac{224p}{3} + 96\).

whyWrong.A: This has no constant term, so the two 12 × 4 faces (96 square centimeters in total) were dropped.
whyWrong.C: This is 2(28p) + 2(96), counting the 12 × 4 face four times and never using the width \(\frac{7p}{3}\).
whyWrong.D: 560p comes from multiplying rather than dividing by the length somewhere; the p-terms should total \(\frac{224p}{3}\).

note: The book's first sentence says "right triangular prism" while the rest of the question and the answer choices are about a right rectangular prism; transcribed as rectangular, which is the reading that makes choice B come out exactly.

stem: Rectangle \(ABCD\) and \(EFGH\) are similar. The length of each side of \(EFGH\) is 6 times the length of the corresponding side of \(ABCD\). The area of \(ABCD\) is 102 square units. What is the area, in square units, of \(EFGH\)?
whyCorrect: Length and width both grow by 6, so the area grows by \(6^2 = 36\): 102 × 36 = 3,672 square units.

whyWrong.A: 17 is 102 ÷ 6 — shrinking rather than enlarging.
whyWrong.B: 36 is the area factor, which still has to multiply 102.
whyWrong.C: 612 is 102 × 6, scaling only one dimension.

stem: A right square pyramid has a height of 11 centimeters (cm). A second right square pyramid has a height of 22 centimeters. The area of the base of each of the two pyramids is 100 \(\text{cm}^2\). Which of the following is closest to the difference in the surface area of the second pyramid and the surface area of the first pyramid, in \(\text{cm}^2\)?
whyCorrect: The bases are identical, so only the lateral faces differ. Each base edge is \(\sqrt{100} = 10\), so half an edge is 5, and each slant height is \(\sqrt{h^2 + 5^2}\): \(\sqrt{146} \approx 12.08\) and \(\sqrt{509} \approx 22.56\). Lateral area is \(4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(10)\ell = 20\ell\), so the difference is \(20(22.56 - 12.08) \approx 209.6\), closest to 209.

whyWrong.B: 220 is 20(22 - 11), using the vertical heights in place of the slant heights. The slant heights are what the face areas depend on.
whyWrong.C: 367 is the volume of the first pyramid, \(\frac{1}{3}(100)(11)\) — a volume, not a surface-area difference.
whyWrong.D: 551 is the entire surface area of the second pyramid; the first pyramid's surface area still has to be subtracted.

stem: A right circular cone has a height of 13 centimeters (cm) and a base with a radius of 6 cm. What is the volume, in \(\text{cm}^3\), of this cone?
whyCorrect: A cone is \(V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(6)^2(13) = \frac{1}{3}\pi(36)(13) = 156\pi\). Square the radius, then take a third.

whyWrong.A: \(26\pi\) is \(2 \times 13\pi\); the base area \(36\pi\) never appears.
whyWrong.B: \(78\pi\) is half of \(156\pi\) — a factor of \(\frac{1}{2}\) was used instead of \(\frac{1}{3}\), or 6 was used instead of \(6^2\).
whyWrong.D: \(468\pi\) is \(\pi r^2 h\), the volume of the cylinder with the same base and height. A cone is a third of that.

stem: A sphere has a radius of \(\frac{8}{3}\) feet. What is the volume, in cubic feet, of the sphere?
whyCorrect: Use \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\) and cube numerator and denominator: \(\left(\frac{8}{3}\right)^3 = \frac{512}{27}\). Then \(V = \frac{4}{3}\pi \cdot \frac{512}{27} = \frac{2048\pi}{81}\).

whyWrong.A: This is \(\pi\) times the reciprocal of the radius; the formula was not used.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{32\pi}{9}\) is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r\) with the radius left uncubed.
whyWrong.C: Nothing in the formula produces \(\frac{17}{3}\); check that you cubed \(\frac{8}{3}\).

stem: The width of a rectangle is 5 centimeters. The length of the rectangle is 30 centimeters longer than the width. What is the area, in square centimeters, of this rectangle?
whyCorrect: "30 longer than the width" makes the length 5 + 30 = 35, not 30. The area is then 35 × 5 = 175 square centimeters.

whyWrong.B: 40 is 5 + 35, the length plus the width, which is half the perimeter.
whyWrong.C: 10 is twice the width; no length has been used.
whyWrong.D: 5 is the width by itself.

stem: A triangular prism has a height of 3 centimeters (cm) and a volume of 60 \(\text{cm}^3\). What is the area, in \(\text{cm}^2\), of the base of the prism? (The volume of a triangular prism is equal to Bh, where B is the area of the base and h is the height of the prism.)
whyCorrect: The formula is given: V = Bh, so B = V ÷ h = 60 ÷ 3 = 20 square centimeters. There is no \(\frac{1}{3}\) here — that factor belongs to pyramids and cones, not prisms.
